plan.topic_summary: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is a core post-training technique for large language models, and its evolving role relative to RL-based alignment, parameter-efficient methods, and in-context learning will shape the competitive dynamics and cost structure of AI model providers over the next 1–5 years.
key_questions: How are major AI companies positioning SFT in their post-training pipelines, and is it becoming a standard commodity step or a differentiating capability?
What is the current cost structure of SFT relative to pre-training and RL-based alignment, and how is it trending?
Is SFT being displaced or augmented by RL-based methods (RLHF, DPO, GRPO) as the primary alignment technique, and what does that imply for data-centric businesses?
How does the availability and quality of human-labeled data constrain SFT at scale, and what are the implications for companies that build data curation as a moat?
Will parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA, adapters) commoditize SFT to the point where it becomes a low-barrier capability accessible to small teams?
How does the rise of agentic AI and tool-use change the role of SFT in model development over a 3–5 year horizon?

gaps: No dedicated finding on SFT scaling laws (how performance scales with data size, model size, or compute); the retrieved paper src_a1093a2aba was not cited in any finding for this purpose
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA, QLoRA) is only mentioned in passing (R7, X1) with no dedicated science finding comparing PEFT to full SFT on quality, cost, and applicability
Market evidence is thin: no revenue figures, market sizing, or growth rates for SFT-specific services or tools; M3 and M5 are low-relevance
S5 (mechanistic understanding of SFT via sparse autoencoders) rests on a single paper, limiting confidence in that specific claim
SFT data contamination (training data leaking into evaluation sets) is not explicitly addressed as a distinct risk from general data corruption (R4)

sources.title: Preserving Diversity in Supervised Fine-Tuning of Large Language Models
sources.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) typically rely on Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) to specialize in downstream tasks, with the Cross Entropy (CE) loss being the de facto choice. However, CE maximizes the likelihood of observed data without accounting for alternative possibilities. As such, CE usually leads to reduced diversity in the model's outputs, which hinders further development that requires sampling to explore better responses. To address this limitation, this paper introduces a new game-theoretic formulation for SFT. In this framework, an auxiliary variable is introduced to regulate the learning process. We prove that the proposed game-theoretic approach connects to the problem of reverse KL minimization with entropy regularization. This regularization prevents over-memorization of training data and promotes output diversity. To implement this framework, we develop GEM, a new training algorithm that is computationally efficient as CE by leveraging some unique properties of LLMs. Empirical studies of pre-trained models from 3B to 70B parameters show that GEM achieves comparable downstream performance to CE while significantly enhancing output diversity. This increased diversity translates to performance gains in test-time compute scaling for chat and code generation tasks. Moreover, we observe that preserving output diversity has the added benefit of mitigating forgetting, as maintaining diverse outputs encourages models to retain pre-trained knowledge throughout the training process.

sources.title: Rotation-Preserving Supervised Fine-Tuning
sources.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) improves in-domain performance but can degrade out-of-domain (OOD) generalization. Prior work suggests that this degradation is related to changes in dominant singular subspaces of pretrained weight matrices. However, directly identifying loss-sensitive directions with Hessian or Fisher information is computationally expensive at LLM scale. In this work, we propose preserving projected rotations in pretrained singular subspaces as an efficient proxy for Fisher-sensitive directions, which we call Rotation-Preserving Supervised Fine-Tuning (RPSFT). RPSFT penalizes changes in the projected top-$k$ singular-vector block of each pretrained weight matrix, limiting unnecessary rotation while preserving task adaptation. Across model families and sizes trained on math reasoning data, RPSFT improves the in-domain/OOD trade-off over standard SFT and strong SFT baselines, better preserves pretrained representations, and provides stronger initializations for downstream RL fine-tuning. Code is available at \href{https://github.com/jinhangzhan/RPSFT.git}{https://github.com/jinhangzhan/RPSFT}.

sources.title: #InsTag: Instruction Tagging for Analyzing Supervised Fine-tuning of Large Language Models
sources.abstract: Foundation language models obtain the instruction-following ability through supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Diversity and complexity are considered critical factors of a successful SFT dataset, while their definitions remain obscure and lack quantitative analyses. In this work, we propose InsTag, an open-set fine-grained tagger, to tag samples within SFT datasets based on semantics and intentions and define instruction diversity and complexity regarding tags. We obtain 6.6K tags to describe comprehensive user queries. Then we analyze popular open-sourced SFT datasets and find that the model ability grows with more diverse and complex data. Based on this observation, we propose a data selector based on InsTag to select 6K diverse and complex samples from open-source datasets and fine-tune models on InsTag-selected data. The resulting models, TagLM, outperform open-source models based on considerably larger SFT data evaluated by MT-Bench, echoing the importance of query diversity and complexity. We open-source InsTag in https://github.com/OFA-Sys/InsTag.

sources.title: Anchored Supervised Fine-Tuning
sources.abstract: Post-training of large language models involves a fundamental trade-off between supervised fine-tuning (SFT), which efficiently mimics demonstrations but tends to memorize, and reinforcement learning (RL), which achieves better generalization at higher computational cost. Dynamic Fine-Tuning (DFT) recently emerged as a promising middle ground, reweighting SFT objectives with token probabilities and achieving improvements in certain reasoning domains, though it exhibits instability in other tasks. We provide a analysis of DFT through the reward-weighted regression (RWR) framework, revealing that it corresponds to a specific auxiliary distribution choice that yields provably tighter RL bounds than standard SFT. However, our analysis also uncovers a critical limitation: this construction lacks distributional anchoring, leading to progressive drift that undermines training stability. To address this, we propose Anchored Supervised Fine-Tuning (ASFT), which augments DFT's reweighting with lightweight KL regularization to preserve tightness while ensuring stability. Empirically, ASFT consistently outperforms both SFT and DFT across mathematical reasoning, medical knowledge grounding, and code generation, achieving substantial improvements with minimal computational overhead. Our RWR framework provides a systematic lens for understanding post-training methods and demonstrates that principled theoretical analysis leads to both stronger guarantees and practical gains. The code is available at https://github.com/zhuchichi56/ASFT.

sources.title: How Abilities in Large Language Models are Affected by Supervised Fine-tuning Data Composition
sources.venue: Proceedings of the conference - Association for Computational Linguistics. Meeting
sources.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) with enormous pre-training tokens and parameters emerge diverse abilities, including math reasoning, codegeneration, and instruction following. These abilities are further enhanced by supervised fine-tuning (SFT). While the open-source community has explored ad-hoc SFT for enhancing individual capabilities, proprietary LLMs exhibit versatility across various skills. Therefore, understanding the facilitation of multiple abilities via SFT is paramount. In this study, we specificially focuses on the interplay of data composition between mathematical reasoning, code generation, and general human-aligning abilities during SFT. We propose four intriguing research questions to explore the association between model performance and various factors including data amount, composition ratio, model size and SFT strategies. Our experiments reveal that distinct capabilities scale differently and larger models generally show superior performance with same amount of data. Mathematical reasoning and code generation consistently improve with increasing data amount, whereas general abilities plateau after roughly a thousand samples. Moreover, we observe data composition appears to enhance various abilities under limited data conditions, yet can lead to performance conflicts when data is plentiful. Our findings also suggest the amount of composition data influences performance more than the composition ratio. In analysis of SFT strategies, we find that sequentially learning multiple skills risks catastrophic forgetting. Our proposed Dual-stage Mixed Fine-tuning (DMT) strategy offers a promising solution to learn multiple abilities with different scaling patterns.

sources.title: Supervised Fine-tuning for Geometry-aware Instruction-following
sources.abstract: We examine a contrastive input encoding scheme for supervised fine-tuning of language models (LMs) that masks the content of incorrect generations up to a classification control token. This small-scale study, using a variation of the classic word ordering diagnostic task, suggests this straightforward approach generally preserves the generation accuracy of supervised fine-tuning that uses only positive examples, while increasing the admission rate of generations in the calibrated high-probability region of a Similarity-Distance-Magnitude (SDM) estimator for binary classification of instruction-following. At the same time, we corroborate existing evidence that constructing a calibrated SDM estimator, which models the geometry of the feature-representation space, is not strictly dependent on specialized fine-tuning of the underlying LM's parameters.

sources.title: A Mechanistic Investigation of Supervised Fine Tuning
sources.abstract: The cosine similarity between a large language model's hidden activations before and after Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) remains very high. This, at first glance, suggests that SFT leaves the model's activation geometry largely undisturbed. However, projecting both sets of activations through a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) pretrained on the base model reveals that the underlying sparse latents diverge significantly. We introduce a novel investigative pipeline which utilizes these pretrained SAEs as a high-resolution diagnostic tool to mechanistically investigate the drivers of this representational divergence. Through our analytical pipeline, we discover task-specific and layer-specific distributions of the precise semantic features that are systematically altered during supervised fine-tuning. We additionally identify a layer-wise update profile specific to safety alignment. All code, experimental scripts, and analysis files associated with this work are publicly available at: https://github.com/ruhzi/sae-investigation.

sources.title: Supervised Fine-Tuning as Inverse Reinforcement Learning
sources.abstract: The prevailing approach to aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) typically relies on human or AI feedback and assumes access to specific types of preference datasets. In our work, we question the efficacy of such datasets and explore various scenarios where alignment with expert demonstrations proves more realistic. We build a sequential decision-making framework to formulate the problem of aligning LLMs using demonstration datasets. Drawing insights from inverse reinforcement learning and imitation learning, we introduce various approaches for divergence minimization in the LLM alignment tasks. Our analysis highlights the mass-covering and mode-seeking behaviors of these different approaches. Inclusively, we examine the pros and cons of the classical supervised fine-tuning method, elaborating on scenarios where different methods shine.

sources.title: Towards Pedagogical LLMs with Supervised Fine Tuning for Computing Education
sources.abstract: This paper investigates supervised fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) to improve their pedagogical alignment in computing education, addressing concerns that LLMs may hinder learning outcomes. The project utilised a proprietary dataset of 2,500 high quality question/answer pairs from programming course forums, and explores two research questions: the suitability of university course forums in contributing to fine-tuning datasets, and how supervised fine-tuning can improve LLMs' alignment with educational principles such as constructivism. Initial findings suggest benefits in pedagogical alignment of LLMs, with deeper evaluations required.

sources.title: Rethinking Data Selection for Supervised Fine-Tuning
sources.abstract: Although supervised finetuning (SFT) has emerged as an essential technique to align large language models with humans, it is considered superficial, with style learning being its nature. At the same time, recent works indicate the importance of data selection for SFT, showing that finetuning with high-quality and diverse subsets of the original dataset leads to superior downstream performance. In this work, we rethink the intuition behind data selection for SFT. Considering SFT is superficial, we propose that essential demonstrations for SFT should focus on reflecting human-like interactions instead of data quality or diversity. However, it is not straightforward to directly assess to what extent a demonstration reflects human styles. Towards an initial attempt in this direction, we find selecting instances with long responses is surprisingly more effective for SFT than utilizing full datasets or instances selected based on quality and diversity. We hypothesize that such a simple heuristic implicitly mimics a crucial aspect of human-style conversation: detailed responses are usually more helpful.

sources.title: Labeling supervised fine-tuning data with the scaling law
sources.abstract: This paper introduces a multi-stage manual annotation calibrated by the scaling law, offering a high-quality Supervised Fine-Tuning data acquisition method for environments with constrained resources like GPU poor, limited GPT access, and funding restrictions. We have preprocessed 58k authentic chat data and manually annotated 2.3k questions. After this, we conducted fine-tuning on Qwen models, ranging from 0.5B to 32B parameters. The optimal version improved 29.07 in F1 score. This confirms the viability of fine-tuning Large Language Model (LLM) for downstream Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks. Our contributions are: 1) Created Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) training data in alpaca format, along with a set of Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) weights, and 2) Developed a method for acquiring high-quality data leveraging scaling law principle. The script, raw data with alpaca format and experiments track are open-sourced on Github (https://github.com/InternLM/HuixiangDou/tree/main/web/tools), HuggingFace (https://huggingface.co/tpoisonooo) and WandB (https://wandb.ai/tpoisonooo/huixiangdou-cr/table?nw=nwusertpoisonooo). The privacy of the data involved has been authorized by users. SFT data and license comes from ncnn contributors group.

sources.title: Unveiling the Secret Recipe: A Guide For Supervised Fine-Tuning Small LLMs
sources.abstract: The rise of large language models (LLMs) has created a significant disparity: industrial research labs with their computational resources, expert teams, and advanced infrastructures, can effectively fine-tune LLMs, while individual developers and small organizations face barriers due to limited resources. In this paper, we aim to bridge this gap by presenting a comprehensive study on supervised fine-tuning of LLMs using instruction-tuning datasets spanning diverse knowledge domains and skills. We focus on small-sized LLMs (3B to 7B parameters) for their cost-efficiency and accessibility. We explore various training configurations and strategies across four open-source pre-trained models. We provide detailed documentation of these configurations, revealing findings that challenge several common training practices, including hyperparameter recommendations from TULU and phased training recommended by Orca. Key insights from our work include: (i) larger batch sizes paired with lower learning rates lead to improved model performance on benchmarks such as MMLU, MTBench, and Open LLM Leaderboard; (ii) early-stage training dynamics, such as lower gradient norms and higher loss values, are strong indicators of better final model performance, enabling early termination of sub-optimal runs and significant computational savings; (iii) through a thorough exploration of hyperparameters like warmup steps and learning rate schedules, we provide guidance for practitioners and find that certain simplifications do not compromise performance; and (iv) we observed no significant difference in performance between phased and stacked training strategies, but stacked training is simpler and more sample efficient. With these findings holding robustly across datasets and models, we hope this study serves as a guide for practitioners fine-tuning small LLMs and promotes a more inclusive environment for LLM research.

findings.claim: Cross-entropy loss in SFT systematically reduces output diversity and causes over-memorization of training data, which is a recognized limitation across multiple independent studies.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: Three independent papers identify this issue. GEM (ICLR 2025) explicitly states CE leads to reduced diversity; ASFT (arXiv preprint) characterizes SFT as tending to memorize; the IRL framing paper (arXiv preprint) discusses mode-seeking behavior of SFT. The preprints are not peer-reviewed but the ICLR paper provides peer-reviewed confirmation.

sources.title: Mechanistic origins of catastrophic forgetting: why RL preserves circuits better than SFT?
sources.abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) frequently induces catastrophic forgetting of prior capabilities. Recent work has shown that reinforcement learning (RL) retains prior capabilities more effectively than supervised fine-tuning (SFT), attributing this to policy-gradient updates remaining closer to the base policy \cite{shenfeld2025rl}. We extend this behavioral account to the mechanistic level and ask whether RL's advantage is mirrored by stronger preservation of internal computational circuits. We introduce differential circuit vulnerability, a head-level measure of how much a circuit degrades under fine-tuning, and use it to compare RL and SFT on Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct adapted to scientific question-answering. We find a clear mechanistic trade-off: SFT adapts more rapidly to the target task but produces substantially greater circuit disruption and forgetting of prior capabilities, whereas RL preserves a larger fraction of the base circuit at the cost of slower task adaptation. These findings suggest that circuit preservation may help explain why RL is more robust to catastrophic forgetting. We released our code here: https://github.com/rl-sft-circuit-research/differential-circuit-vulnerability.

sources.title: Sensitivity of Small Language Models to Fine-tuning Data Contamination
sources.abstract: Small Language Models (SLMs) are increasingly being deployed in resource-constrained environments, yet their behavioral robustness to data contamination during instruction tuning remains poorly understood. We systematically investigate the contamination sensitivity of 23 SLMs (270M to 4B parameters) across multiple model families by measuring susceptibility to syntactic and semantic transformation types during instruction tuning: syntactic transformations (character and word reversal) and semantic transformations (irrelevant and counterfactual responses), each applied at contamination levels of 25\%, 50\%, 75\%, and 100\%. Our results reveal fundamental asymmetries in vulnerability patterns: syntactic transformations cause catastrophic performance degradation, with character reversal producing near-complete failure across all models regardless of size or family, while semantic transformations demonstrate distinct threshold behaviors and greater resilience in core linguistic capabilities. Critically, we discover a ``\textit{capability curse}" where larger, more capable models become more susceptible to learning semantic corruptions, effectively following harmful instructions more readily, while our analysis of base versus instruction-tuned variants reveals that alignment provides inconsistent robustness benefits, sometimes even reducing resilience. Our work establishes three core contributions: (1) empirical evidence of SLMs' disproportionate vulnerability to syntactic pattern contamination, (2) identification of asymmetric sensitivity patterns between syntactic and semantic transformations, and (3) systematic evaluation protocols for contamination robustness assessment. These findings have immediate deployment implications, suggesting that current robustness assumptions may not hold for smaller models and highlighting the need for contamination-aware training protocols.

sources.title: Improved Supervised Fine-Tuning for Large Language Models to Mitigate Catastrophic Forgetting
sources.abstract: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is a critical step for enhancing the instruction-following capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) and adapting them to specialized domains. However, SFT often leads to a degradation of the model's general abilities, a phenomenon known as catastrophic forgetting. This problem is exacerbated when third-party practitioners fine-tune open-source models, as the original SFT data is typically not available. To address this challenge, we propose a novel and cost-effective SFT method that effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting without requiring access to the original SFT data. Our approach first reconstructs the likely instruction distribution of the base model. It then employs a multi-model generation and filtering pipeline to synthesize a high-quality general-purpose dataset. This synthetic dataset is mixed with new, domain-specific data for fine-tuning. Experimental results show that our method not only preserves the model's capabilities in general domains but also improves task-specific performance, outperforming baselines that use publicly available SFT datasets.

sources.title: Retaining by Doing: The Role of On-Policy Data in Mitigating Forgetting
sources.abstract: Adapting language models (LMs) to new tasks via post-training carries the risk of degrading existing capabilities -- a phenomenon classically known as catastrophic forgetting. In this paper, toward identifying guidelines for mitigating this phenomenon, we systematically compare the forgetting patterns of two widely adopted post-training methods: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL). Our experiments reveal a consistent trend across LM families (Llama, Qwen) and tasks (instruction following, general knowledge, and arithmetic reasoning): RL leads to less forgetting than SFT while achieving comparable or higher target task performance. To investigate the cause for this difference, we consider a simplified setting in which the LM is modeled as a mixture of two distributions, one corresponding to prior knowledge and the other to the target task. We identify that the mode-seeking nature of RL, which stems from its use of on-policy data, enables keeping prior knowledge intact when learning the target task. We then verify this insight by demonstrating that the use on-policy data underlies the robustness of RL to forgetting in practical settings, as opposed to other algorithmic choices such as the KL regularization or advantage estimation. Lastly, as a practical implication, our results highlight the potential of mitigating forgetting using approximately on-policy data, which can be substantially more efficient to obtain than fully on-policy data.

sources.title: CPR for LLMs: Critical-Point Routing against Catastrophic Forgetting in Domain Adaptation
sources.venue: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP)
sources.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is the de facto standard for adapting large language models (LLMs) to target domains, but it often degrades the model’s general capabilities, a phenomenon known as catastrophic forgetting. Existing approaches typically modify the SFT loss to mitigate forgetting, but they inevitably operate along a domain-generality trade-off. In this work, we step outside this trade-off by decoupling the two capabilities at the model level: we keep the original base model for general capability, and selectively invoke the SFT expert only when domain-specific knowledge is required. Specifically, we propose CPR ( C ritical- P oint R outing), a token-level routing framework between a base model and its expert derivative, based on critical tokens where the base model fails but the expert succeeds. We train a lightweight hierarchical router that estimates the expert-call probability per token, and pair it with a tailored inference procedure that combines momentum smoothing and threshold gating. Across diverse model-domain configurations, CPR achieves state-of-the-art across all settings, surpassing SFT expert by 1.4-5.5% in domain performance while recovering its general-capability drop from 3.4-14.5% to at most 0.5%, with minimal overhead from invoking the expert on only one-third of tokens.

sources.title: SFT-as-Context Mitigates Forgetting in Supervised Fine-Tuning
sources.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) equips large language models (LLMs) with specialized capabilities, but often comes at the cost of forgetting the general capabilities of their parent models (i.e., the pretrained models before fine-tuning). This trade-off is especially limiting for queries that require both specialized and general capabilities. We introduce SFT-as-context, a training-free method in which the parent model uses the SFT model's response as context to answer the query. This allows the parent model to acquire fine-tuned capabilities from the SFT response through in-context learning while preserving its own general capabilities. Across 19 parent-SFT model pairs and 11 benchmarks, SFT-as-context remains close to the SFT models on fine-tuned capabilities, with gaps of only 2.2 and 2.1 percentage points on AIME 2024 and LiveCodeBench and 2.0 macro MAE on NutriBench-English, while staying within 2.2 percentage points of the parent models on general capabilities on average. Remarkably, it can solve queries requiring both fine-tuned and general capabilities, even when neither the parent nor SFT model succeeds alone. This approach also extends beyond parent-SFT pairs: responses from a small open-source SFT model can improve a strong closed-source LLM, outperforming either model alone. Furthermore, we use a Bayesian framework to derive theoretical guarantees that bound the error of SFT-as-context relative to the SFT model on fine-tuned capabilities and to the parent model on general capabilities. In addition, we visualize the attention weights and find that the parent model attends more to useful SFT responses and less to irrelevant ones, suggesting that selective attention helps the parent model use the SFT response through in-context learning.

sources.title: (How) Learning Rates Regulate Catastrophic Overtraining
sources.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is a common first stage of LLM post-training, teaching the model to follow instructions and shaping its behavior as a helpful assistant. At the same time, SFT may harm the fundamental capabilities of an LLM, particularly after long pretraining: a phenomenon known as catastrophic overtraining (Springer et al., 2025). To understand overtraining, we first investigate catastrophic forgetting in finetuning through the lens of implicit regularization of the learning rate. For models trained to the same SFT loss, we identify how the learning rate mediates optimization: finetuning with large and small steps converges to qualitatively different models. Next, we link forgetting to overtraining: learning rate decay increases the sharpness of the pretrained model, which in turn exacerbates catastrophic forgetting during SFT, leading to overtraining. Our findings paint a picture of the overtraining mechanism in LLMs and broadly contribute to the understanding of the interplay between optimization dynamics during pretraining and finetuning.

sources.title: A Comparative Analysis of LLM Adaptation: SFT, LoRA, and ICL in Data-Scarce Scenarios
sources.abstract: The remarkable capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) often need to be tailored for specific applications, requiring the integration of new knowledge or the acquisition of new skills. While full fine-tuning is a powerful adaptation method, it is computationally expensive and can lead to a degradation of general reasoning abilities, a phenomenon known as catastrophic forgetting. A range of alternative techniques exists, each with its own trade-offs. In-Context Learning (ICL) is fast but limited by context length, while Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods like Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) offer a middle ground by minimizing parameter changes. However, the challenge of catastrophic forgetting persists, raising questions about the best adaptation strategy for a given task. This paper presents a comparative analysis of Supervised Finetuning (SFT), LoRA, and ICL in data-scarce scenarios. We find that LoRA provides the most effective balance, successfully instilling new skills with minimal impact on the base model's general knowledge. In contrast, while SFT excels at skill acquisition, it is highly susceptible to catastrophic forgetting. ICL is effective for incorporating factual knowledge but struggles with complex skills. Our findings offer a practical framework for selecting an LLM adaptation strategy. We highlight the critical distinction between skill acquisition and knowledge integration, clarify the trade-offs between task-specific performance and the preservation of general capabilities.

sources.title: Biological Continued Pretraining Reshapes the Capability Profile of a Foundation Model Without Catastrophic Forgetting
sources.abstract: It is widely assumed that continued pretraining (CPT) on a narrow, out-of-distribution corpus such as raw biological sequence must trade away a general-purpose model’s broad competence — the “alignment tax” or catastrophic-forgetting intuition. We test this directly, without any new training, by re-analyzing three checkpoints from a single lineage of a 26B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model (Gemma-4-26B-A4B): the instruction-tuned base, the same model after biological CPT (8.7B tokens of DNA, protein, and biomedical text), and after subsequent supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Across three independent capability axes — general knowledge/reasoning (MMLU, ARC, HellaSwag), code generation (MBPP), and biomedical knowledge (BixBench) — we find that biological CPT does not degrade the model; it lifts it: MMLU +13 points, MBPP pass@1 nearly doubles (0.33 →0.63), and BixBench discrimination rises sharply (MCC 0.23 → 0.92). The single measured regression is truthfulness (TruthfulQA 8.8 points), a small and interpretable domain drift. A clean vocabulary-expansion ablation (< 0.4 pt on every general metric) confirms the gains are attributable to CPT, not tokenizer changes. Crucially, subsequent SFT narrows the model back: all three axes fall to near-base levels, revealing a consistent division of labor — CPT re-organizes and lifts the shared capability substrate; SFT cashes it out onto target tasks. We argue this reframes biological sequence not as a competitor for a foundation model’s capacity but as a form of structured scientific data that reshapes its capability profile, and that CPT and SFT should be budgeted as complementary rather than substitutable stages. All checkpoints, evaluation code, and per-example outputs are public. Highlights A training-free re-analysis of one 26B MoE lineage isolates the effect of biological continued pretraining (CPT) from tokenizer changes and from fine-tuning. Biological CPT does not cause catastrophic forgetting; it raises general knowledge (MMLU +13 pts) and code generation (MBPP pass@1 0.33 → 0.63). CPT also makes chain-of-thought reasoning 41% shorter and near-backtrack-free while pre-serving accuracy — an effect invisible to accuracy metrics. A consistent CPT-lifts / SFT-narrows division of labor recurs across four axes, reframing biological sequence as structured scientific data that reshapes a model’s capability profile. The Bigger Picture Adapting a general-purpose AI model to a specialized domain — here, the language of DNA and proteins — is usually assumed to come at a cost: teach it biology and it forgets how to reason about everything else. This “no free lunch” intuition shapes how practitioners budget compute and whether they attempt domain adaptation at all. We test the assumption directly, and without running any new training, by comparing three snapshots of the same model taken before and after biological training. The result overturns the intuition: feeding the model raw biological sequence made it better at general knowledge, at writing code, and even changed how it reasons — producing shorter, more decisive chains of thought without losing accuracy. The gains appear during the sequence-pretraining stage and are partly given back during task-specific fine-tuning, revealing that the two stages play complementary rather than interchangeable roles. This suggests a broader principle for data-centric AI: structured scientific data — biological sequence today, and by extension code, mathematics, and chemistry — is not merely knowledge to be absorbed but a lever that reshapes what a foundation model can do.

sources.title: TMS: Trajectory-Mixed Supervision for Reward-Free, On-Policy SFT
sources.abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) are the two dominant paradigms for enhancing Large Language Model (LLM) performance on downstream tasks. While RL generally preserves broader model capabilities (retention) better than SFT, it comes with significant costs: complex reward engineering, instability, and expensive on-policy sampling. In contrast, SFT is efficient but brittle, often suffering from catastrophic forgetting due to $\textbf{Supervision Mismatch}$: the divergence between the model's evolving policy and static training labels. We address this trade-off with $\textbf{Trajectory-Mixed Supervision (TMS)}$, a reward-free framework that approximates the on-policy benefits of RL by creating a dynamic curriculum from the model's own historical checkpoints. TMS minimizes $\textit{Policy-Label Divergence (PLD)}$, preventing the mode collapse that drives forgetting in standard SFT. Experiments across reasoning (MATH, GSM8K) and instruction-following benchmarks demonstrate that TMS effectively shifts the accuracy--retention Pareto frontier. While RL remains the gold standard for retention, TMS significantly outperforms standard and iterative SFT, bridging the gap to RL without requiring reward models or verifiers. Mechanistic analysis confirms that PLD drift accurately predicts forgetting and that TMS successfully mitigates this drift.

sources.title: Entropic Control for Homeostatic Optimization: Pre-empting Catastrophic Forgetting via Dynamic Feedback
sources.abstract: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) of LLMs suffers from catastrophic forgetting, and prevailing mitigation strategies struggle to reconcile the plasticity-stability dilemma. To address this, we propose Entropic Control for Homeostatic Optimization (ECHO), a closed-loop control framework. By decomposing the KL divergence, we identify output entropy as a dominant observable component of KL variation. This enables us to leverage entropy as a computationally efficient online proxy to monitor forgetting risks in real-time, bypassing expensive reference-model inference. Consequently, ECHO employs an elastic controller that dynamically modulates the gradient weight of replay data via a proportional control law, using deviations from the pre-trained entropic equilibrium as an error signal. Empirical evaluations across 0.6B to 9B parameter architectures demonstrate that ECHO lies on, and in several comparisons extends, the observed plasticity-stability frontier and maintains high operational robustness against varying data mixing ratios.

sources.title: Robust Policy Optimization to Prevent Catastrophic Forgetting
sources.abstract: Large language models are commonly trained through multi-stage post-training: first via RLHF, then fine-tuned for other downstream objectives. Yet even small downstream updates can compromise earlier learned behaviors (e.g., safety), exposing a brittleness known as catastrophic forgetting. This suggests standard RLHF objectives do not guarantee robustness to future adaptation. To address it, most prior work designs downstream-time methods to preserve previously learned behaviors. We argue that preventing this requires pre-finetuning robustness: the base policy should avoid brittle high-reward solutions whose reward drops sharply under standard fine-tuning. We propose Fine-tuning Robust Policy Optimization (FRPO), a robust RLHF framework that optimizes reward not only at the current policy, but across a KL-bounded neighborhood of policies reachable by downstream adaptation. The key idea is to ensure reward stability under policy shifts via a max-min formulation. By modifying GRPO, we develop an algorithm with no extra computation, and empirically show it substantially reduces safety degradation across multiple base models and downstream fine-tuning regimes (SFT and RL) while preserving downstream task performance. We further study a math-focused RL setting, demonstrating that FRPO preserves accuracy under subsequent fine-tuning.

findings.claim: Standard SFT is repeatedly reported to degrade a model's prior capabilities, and RL post-training is reported to forget less. This is a risk that SFT-based adaptation could be displaced or require a more complex pipeline.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: Three papers point the same way: Llama and Qwen families in src_66352e99f1, and a single Qwen2.5-3B model in src_f3090a8ebb. The mechanistic circuit result in src_f3090a8ebb is narrow (one model, one scientific QA task) and is an arXiv preprint, not peer reviewed. src_ecf3be4fc7 is a method paper that also treats SFT as brittle. Evidence is from abstracts only.
findings.supporting_excerpt: RL leads to less forgetting than SFT while achieving comparable or higher target task performance

findings.claim: RL is not a free replacement for SFT. The papers describe slower task adaptation and engineering and compute costs, so the SFT-versus-RL trade-off remains unresolved.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: src_f3090a8ebb (arXiv preprint, one 3B model) reports that RL preserves more of the base circuit but adapts more slowly. src_ecf3be4fc7 says RL carries 'complex reward engineering, instability, and expensive on-policy sampling'. src_66352e99f1 reports RL reaching comparable or higher target performance, which partly contradicts the slower-adaptation finding. The contradiction may reflect different models and tasks, and the abstracts do not resolve it.

findings.claim: Optimization settings and pretraining history can make SFT forget more. Learning-rate decay in pretraining is linked to higher sharpness of the pretrained model and worse forgetting during SFT ('catastrophic overtraining'). Forgetting therefore depends on factors outside the fine-tuning dataset.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: Single arXiv preprint, abstract only. The scope of models and scales tested is not visible, so generality is unknown. This is a mechanism-level claim, not a measured market effect.
findings.supporting_excerpt: learning rate decay increases the sharpness of the pretrained model, which in turn exacerbates catastrophic forgetting during SFT, leading to overtraining.

findings.claim: Instruction-tuning small language models is highly sensitive to corrupted training data. Character reversal caused near-complete failure in all 23 models tested. Larger, more capable models more readily learned semantic corruptions, and alignment gave inconsistent robustness.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: arXiv preprint, abstract only, and the abstract is truncated. The contamination types (reversal, irrelevant and counterfactual responses) are synthetic, so how well they reflect real-world data-quality problems is a gap. The 'capability curse' result is interesting but rests on one study.
findings.supporting_excerpt: syntactic transformations cause catastrophic performance degradation, with character reversal producing near-complete failure across all models regardless of size or family

findings.claim: Fine-tuning can erode earlier-learned safety behaviour. Even small downstream updates can compromise it, and the proposed fix must be applied before fine-tuning (at the base-model training stage), which a third-party fine-tuner may not control.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: The abstract states that even small downstream updates can compromise earlier learned behaviors such as safety. FRPO requires changing RLHF at the base-policy stage, so it only helps if the model developer adopts it. That second point is my inference. The result is an arXiv preprint and the abstract gives no figures, so the size of the effect is unknown.

findings.claim: Many proposed forgetting mitigations add pipeline complexity, require a second model at inference, or still leave a measurable gap. This suggests the forgetting problem is not solved.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: CPR (src_7f785c6dda) keeps a base model plus an expert model and a router, and the general-capability drop is still reported as 'at most 0.5%'. SFT-as-context (src_fe0bb1978f) needs both a parent and an SFT model at inference and stays about 2 points below the SFT model on fine-tuned capabilities. src_7205f92b15 needs a synthetic-data generation and filtering pipeline because original SFT data is often unavailable to third parties. src_afd45958a9 (preprint) adds a control loop over replay data. src_ecf3be4fc7 states RL remains the gold standard for retention. The added serving and engineering cost is my inference, since the abstracts do not quantify it. All results are self-reported by the method authors on their chosen benchmarks, and several are arXiv preprints.

findings.claim: Full SFT is reported to be highly susceptible to forgetting compared with LoRA and in-context learning in data-scarce settings. Parameter-efficient or prompting alternatives could displace full SFT there, though each has its own limits.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: Single arXiv preprint, abstract only, restricted to data-scarce scenarios, so it should not be generalized to large-data SFT. The same abstract says ICL struggles with complex skills and that SFT is strongest for skill acquisition.
findings.supporting_excerpt: while SFT excels at skill acquisition, it is highly susceptible to catastrophic forgetting.

findings.claim: SFT may erase capability gains made by earlier training stages. In one re-analysis, a subsequent SFT step returned a model's capability axes to near-base levels after biological continued pretraining had lifted them. The evidence base is one model lineage.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: bioRxiv preprint, not peer reviewed. It re-analyzes three checkpoints of a single 26B MoE lineage without new training, so reproducibility and generality are open. The paper's main claim is that CPT does not cause forgetting, which also conflicts with the common 'alignment tax' view. The SFT narrowing is a side observation and was not necessarily the focus of the study.
findings.supporting_excerpt: Crucially, subsequent SFT narrows the model back: all three axes fall to near-base levels

hype_flags: 'State-of-the-art across all settings' (CPR): self-reported by the method authors on their own configurations, with no independent replication visible in the abstract.
'Bridging the gap to RL' (TMS): the same abstract concedes RL remains the gold standard for retention.
'Remarkably, it can solve queries requiring both fine-tuned and general capabilities' (SFT-as-context): an authors' framing of benchmark results from an unreviewed preprint.
Mechanistic explanation of why RL preserves circuits better than SFT: based on one 3B model on one task domain, so it is premature to generalize.
'CPT without catastrophic forgetting' and 'lifts the model': a re-analysis of one model lineage, and it also shows a TruthfulQA regression.
Claims that forgetting is solved or 'on the frontier': ECHO and similar papers compare against chosen baselines, and many cited works are arXiv preprints with 0-8 citations.

finding.claim: S1 is labelled verified_fact/high and says SFT 'systematically' reduces diversity and causes over-memorization, 'across multiple independent studies'. The cited abstracts do not show this. The GEM paper (src_ee58cdf370) states the diversity loss as the motivation for its own method, hedged with 'usually'. The Anchored SFT paper says only that SFT 'tends to memorize', as framing for its proposal. The IRL paper (src_f9645a8cde) is a theoretical comparison of mass-covering and mode-seeking divergences; its abstract makes no claim that SFT reduces diversity. The independent evidence is therefore one paper's empirical result (GEM) plus introductory framing in the other two.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: Problem statements in papers that propose fixes are not independent replications. The IRL paper's focus on mass-covering behaviour sits uneasily with a blanket claim of diversity collapse, since mass-covering objectives are usually associated with broader coverage. The abstract does not say which behaviour it attributes to SFT. The claim should be downgraded from verified_fact and qualified (e.g. 'reported by GEM authors, in 3B-70B chat/code settings').

finding.claim: S2 groups three methods as mitigations for 'SFT's memorization and diversity loss', but the cited abstracts target different problems. Rotation-Preserving SFT targets out-of-domain generalization loss tied to singular-subspace rotation, and does not mention diversity or memorization. Anchored SFT targets training instability and drift in Dynamic Fine-Tuning. Only GEM addresses diversity. Both of the other two are single-author-group arXiv preprints with no citation history and self-reported gains.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The RPSFT abstract frames its problem as OOD degradation, not diversity loss or memorization. The finding presents a unified family of solutions to one problem that the sources do not establish. It reads better as a set of loosely related robustness methods.
finding.supporting_excerpt: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) improves in-domain performance but can degrade out-of-domain (OOD) generalization.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S3 cites 'Rethinking Data Selection for SFT' (src_6fd451c525) as support for the claim that diversity and complexity are critical, but that paper argues the opposite. It finds that simply selecting long responses beats selection by quality and diversity. S3 also leaves out that the composition paper (src_3aac71e3ec) reports the amount of composition data matters more than the composition ratio, and that mixing can cause 'performance conflicts when data is plentiful'. The 'critical factors' claim rests mainly on InsTag, which is the source of that proposed definition and is evaluated on MT-Bench.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: One of the three cited papers contradicts the headline claim, so the evidence on the importance of diversity is contested, not settled. S3 should note the dispute and the dependence on the benchmark used.
finding.supporting_excerpt: we find selecting instances with long responses is surprisingly more effective for SFT than utilizing full datasets or instances selected based on quality and diversity.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S8 says empirical evidence shows SFT 'goes beyond surface style', but none of the cited abstracts tests the superficial-alignment hypothesis. The composition paper (src_3aac71e3ec) only shows that math and code scores rise with more SFT data. That is compatible with SFT eliciting skills already present from pretraining. The GEM paper (src_ee58cdf370) concerns diversity and is not relevant to this question. The only paper that addresses the 'superficial' view (src_6fd451c525) endorses it as its premise.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: Improved benchmark scores do not distinguish new capability from elicitation of existing capability. S8 turns this inference into a claim of contested-and-refuted without direct evidence in the cited abstracts.

finding.claim: S5 is a medium-confidence verified_fact built on one arXiv preprint seen only through its abstract. The 'significant divergence' in sparse latents is measured with an SAE pretrained on the base model. A base-model SAE may reconstruct fine-tuned activations poorly, so some of the divergence could be SAE transfer error and not real feature change. The abstract does not rule this out. It also does not say which models or tasks were tested. The conclusion that SFT's effects are 'more subtle than activation-level metrics suggest' goes beyond the abstract.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The risk of an SAE-transfer artifact is my inference, not a stated result. The finding should be caveated as single-source and methodology-dependent.
finding.supporting_excerpt: projecting both sets of activations through a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) pretrained on the base model reveals that the underlying sparse latents diverge significantly.

finding.claim: S6 presents 'SFT efficiency vs RL generalization' as an established central tension and says hybrids 'bridge the gap'. The cited sources are Anchored SFT and Rotation-Preserving SFT, both unreviewed preprints whose gains are self-reported and whose framing of RL generalization appears as introductory context. The finding omits the closest evidence on the trade-off, which is about forgetting. RL forgets less than SFT but adapts more slowly (src_66352e99f1, src_f3090a8ebb). The abstracts therefore do not support equating the tension with 'generalization' or calling it resolved.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The tension is better characterised as efficiency and adaptation speed versus retention. TMS (src_ecf3be4fc7) says RL 'remains the gold standard for retention', so bridging is partial at best.
finding.supporting_excerpt: RL leads to less forgetting than SFT while achieving comparable or higher target task performance.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: The findings do not cover catastrophic forgetting, the most heavily evidenced SFT risk in the retrieved set. S1 and S2 describe SFT's weaknesses only as diversity loss and memorization. Several retrieved papers report that standard SFT degrades prior capabilities, and that this depends on pretraining history and learning rate (src_4e0f384c96). Because of this omission, the practical guidance in S7 (larger batch sizes and lower learning rates) is not weighed against forgetting.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: This is a scope gap. It is relevant because the recommended hyperparameters and data-selection strategies in S3 and S7 were evaluated on benchmark performance, and the abstracts do not say whether retention was measured.
finding.supporting_excerpt: However, SFT often leads to a degradation of the model's general abilities, a phenomenon known as catastrophic forgetting.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S7 turns one empirical study into general practical guidance. The study covers four open-source models at 3B-7B. It is tested on MMLU, MTBench and the Open LLM Leaderboard, and its authors frame the results as challenging TULU and Orca recommendations. 'Larger batch sizes with lower learning rates' and the early-stopping signals are not shown to transfer to other model families, larger models, or other data mixes. Early signals such as higher loss values predicting better final performance are counterintuitive and have no replication in the retrieved set.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The claim is reported accurately but its generality is overstated. It is a single-study result seen through its abstract only.

limitations: Only 12 papers were available, and only titles and abstracts were read (text_depth abstract_only). Some abstracts are truncated, so details of experiments and caveats may be missing.

Most evidence is on LLM post-training (catastrophic forgetting). Topics such as SFT data cost, labeling quality at scale, compute cost, benchmark contamination and security or poisoning are barely covered by this set, so their absence is a coverage gap, not evidence of no risk.
Many papers are arXiv or bioRxiv preprints and are not peer reviewed. Several mitigation papers are authored by the proposers of the methods and use self-selected baselines.
Model sizes studied are often small (0.27B to 9B parameters, or one 26B MoE), so applicability to frontier-scale models is unknown.
No papers addressed commercial adoption, vendors or market dynamics, so no company-level risks are stated.
Citation counts and venue metadata (for example a very high count for a recently dated ICML paper) look inconsistent and were not used as evidence.
Only titles and abstracts were available, so I cannot check experimental details, baselines, or whether the papers contain caveats that the abstracts omit.
Several retrieved abstracts are truncated, so some claims may be qualified in the missing text.
The evidence set is small (24 papers) and skewed toward forgetting and mitigation papers. I could not check whether other papers contradict or support S1, S4 or S5.
Many sources are recent arXiv preprints with no citation history, and I could not assess their peer-review status.

I did not challenge S4's core claim that SFT can be framed as inverse reinforcement learning and reward-weighted regression, since the abstracts support it. I only noted that these are separate frameworks, which is a minor point.

sources.title: MENTALESE: A FRAMEWORK TO TRAIN ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI) MODELS TO REASON IN A COMPACT STYLE [US20260369395A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    A computer-implemented method receives an input query and generates, by a machine learning model, a compressed reasoning trace comprising a sequence of symbolic reasoning steps. Individual symbolic reasoning steps comprise an operator token selected from a set of predefined reasoning operators and a symbolic expression token encoding a logical operation without natural language words. The compressed reasoning trace has a compressed token count that is less than a natural language token count of a natural language reasoning trace produced by a natural language model in response to the same input query, reducing inference-time computational load. The method identifies an answer operator in the compressed reasoning trace indicating that the compressed reasoning trace has concluded and extracts a final answer from an answer expression corresponding to the answer operator. A multi-stage training process comprising supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning trains the machine learning model to generate compressed reasoning traces.

sources.title: FINE-TUNING OR TRAINING LANGUAGE MODELS WITH DATA SELECTION [US20260368544A1]
sources.abstract: The embodiments herein describe a bilevel data selector that can rank or score training samples based on a desired criteria (e.g., safety, legal compliance, correctness, etc.). A user can then filter the ranked training samples (e.g., only using training samples with a rank above a threshold, or only using the top 40% of training samples) to then perform fine-tuning of an already trained LLM (referred to as post training) or perform the initial training of a untrained LLM (referred to as pre-training). That is, the data selector uses a bilevel optimization to up rank (or score higher) the safe and high-quality training samples and down rank the unsafe or low-quality samples. The embodiments herein also describe different techniques for training a bilevel data selector.

sources.title: Systems and Methods for Fine-Tuning Generative Models for Detecting the Relevance of Content Items [US20260368531A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    Systems and methods for fine-tuning a generative model for detecting the relevance of content items are provided. The method includes receiving, by a computing system, a website identifier associated with a web resource; extracting, by the computing system, a plurality of assets from the web resource based on the website identifier; generating, by a first machine-learning model operating on the computing system, a summarization of the web resource based on the plurality of assets; processing, by a second machine-learning model operating on the computing system, the summarization of the web resource to generate a content item; and processing, by a large language model (LLM) operating on the computing system, the content item to generate a binary content score based on the summarization of the web resource.

In one aspect, a method is disclosed that includes accessing example pairs comprising code examples and results associated with performance of a code task on corresponding code examples, generating, by a generative model, a specification and edge and corner case definitions for each of the example pairs, generating, by a generative model, a set of preference alignment training examples comprises versions of results associated with the code examples based on the example pairs and the specification for each of the example pairs, and fine-tuning a machine learning model with the set of preference alignment training examples.

sources.title: VERIFIED STATIC CONTENT-BASED SELF-OPTIMIZING AI RESPONSE SYSTEM [WO2026240285A1]
sources.abstract: The present invention relates to an AI-based response system that generates natural language responses to user queries by integrating verified static content to produce reliable and structured outputs. The system dynamically adjusts the balance between information accuracy and expression style through a nonlinear self-regulation mechanism driven by internal feedback generated from verified content. This mechanism enables rapid adaptation in early stages and gradual fine-tuning near optimal states. A composite evaluation index is used to prioritize and organize semantic blocks in the response. Verified content is integrated through appropriate methods—such as inline insertion, footnotes, or dedicated sections—to enhance clarity and reliability. This system autonomously improves response quality using internal feedback without relying on user input, enabling adaptive optimization aligned with domain-specific requirements.

sources.abstract: This method may comprise a step in which a user terminal acquires a base AI model from a server. The base AI model may be acquired from a server. The method may comprise a step in which the user terminal acquires a personalized AI model by fine-tuning the base AI model on the basis of user data. The user data may be collected in a process of executing the base AI model in the user terminal. The method may comprise a step in which the user terminal generates model-specific information corresponding to the personalized AI model on the basis of unique properties of the user terminal. The method may comprise a step in which the user terminal performs signing on the personalized AI model by using the model-specific information. The method may comprise a step in which the user terminal transmits the model-specific information and the signed personalized AI model to the server.

sources.title: AGENTIC CODE ATTESTATION [WO2026241060A1]
sources.abstract: A system and method for prompting and orchestrating a series of artificial intelligence (Al) agents to evaluate the safety of arbitrary code relative to a data owner's own policies around data access and sharing by other parties in a data cleanroom replaces the need for humans to audit and understand arbitrary code before executing it on sensitive datasets. Instead, specialized models are deployed to evaluate code for adherence to compliance regimes, privacy controls, and other security constraints as described in policy inputs from data owners. These functions are performed without needing to access source data and without internalizing the actual submitted code, such that data owners can make a value judgment on whether to allow code to execute on their data without needing to directly audit the code. The code developers have assurance that only a machine is evaluating their code, with no fine-tuning, such that there is no risk of IP leakage due to the evaluation being performed.

sources.title: SYSTEMS AND METHODS FOR ENHANCING LARGE LANGUAGE MODEL RELIABILITY WITH HALLUCINATION AVERSE FINE-TUNING AND DETECTION [US20260359628A1]
sources.abstract: A method may include: receiving, by a computer program, pairs of conversation text and summaries; generating, by the computer program, training data by injecting hallucinations into the conversation text or the summaries; fine-tuning, by the computer program, a large language model (LLM) with the generated training data using a loss function; providing, by the computer program, validation conversation text to the fine-tuned LLM; generating, by the computer program, a lookback ratio vector comprising attention paid by the fine-tuned LLM to content at each token generation step; extracting, by the computer program, token probabilities at each layer of the fine-tuned LLM into a logit-based vector; concatenating, by the computer program, the lookback ratio vector and the logit-based vector; classifying, by the computer program, the concatenated lookback ratio vector and the logit-based vector using a logistic regression classifier; and deploying, by the computer program, the LLM to a production environment.

sources.title: SYSTEMS AND METHODS FOR PERSONALIZING A VIRTUAL AGENT TRAINED USING AN ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI) MODEL [US20260359564A1]
sources.abstract: A computer implemented method is provided for automatically generating a textual response to a message using a trained artificial intelligence (AI) model. The method includes receiving a request to customize the trained AI model and initiating a training phase comprising parsing the request to generate a set of fine-tuning parameters. The fine-tuning parameters include one or more of (i) a contextual prompt configured to capture a guardrail for specifying a desired subject matter within which the response falls, and (ii) a vector-based representation of a desired tone for the response. The method further includes generating the textual response to the message by inputting the message and the set of fine-tuning parameters into the trained AI model.

sources.title: RETRACTABLE TRAILER HITCH SYSTEMS AND METHODS [US20260356142A1]
sources.abstract: A hitch system can include a ball hitch and an actuator. The actuator can be operated to cause the ball hitch to extend and retract. The ball hitch can include a ball mount and a shank. The hitch system can further include a sleeve configured to telescopingly receive at least a portion of the shank. In this manner, a position of the ball hitch can be adjusted with respect to a towing vehicle for “fine tuning” a position of the ball hitch when coupling, decoupling, and/or moving a towed vehicle (e.g., a trailer).

sources.title: SYSTEMS AND METHODS FOR JOINT FINE-TUNING AND COMPRESSION OF NEURAL NETWORKS [WO2026235215A1]
sources.abstract: A method and system are provided for constructing neural network models optimized for reduced computational resource usage. A weight matrix of a neural network layer is represented as a parameterized, compressible data structure comprising learnable parameters. A composite objective function is determined, including a task loss component measuring predictive performance and a compression loss component penalizing resource usage characteristics such as parameter dimensionality, sparsity, or numerical precision, for the neural network model. The neural network model is iteratively optimized with respect to the composite objective function using gradient-based updates to the compressible structure. The resulting model achieves both accuracy and efficiency objectives during a shared optimization process. The optimized compressible data structure may be adapted for different target tasks, enabling task-specific architectures with reduced inference cost. The trained neural network model is deployable in various environments without reliance on fixed, pretrained components used during optimization.

sources.abstract: A system and method are disclosed for a data curation process that integrates generative models, automated evaluators, and iterative refinement workflows. Input seeds, comprising structured metadata and domain-specific attributes, are evaluated against predefined criteria to generate augmented input-output pairs. These pairs undergo multi-stage evaluation and annotation processes involving corrections, metadata additions, and structured feedback to ensure quality, relevance, and compliance with user-defined standards. Annotated pairs are validated using additional evaluators before being used to train generative models, optimizing their outputs for subsequent tasks. Preference data is dynamically generated across stages to fine-tune models and evaluators, while failed examples are used to generate unit test cases for improving evaluation frameworks. The system incorporates iterative feedback loops to refine input seeds, augmentation prompts, and evaluation criteria, enabling scalable, efficient, and high-quality data curation workflows adaptable to diverse tasks and requirements.

Training the trained driving policy using a machine learning technique and the subset of trajectories 304. The method may use a large language model (LLM). [Figure 3]

sources.title: Method of collecting contextual behavioral data within digital narrative intelligence environments [US12792581B1]
sources.abstract: A computer-implemented narrative intelligence system and method for managing digital artifacts and harvesting contextualized collaborator behaviors to support AI-assisted information management and model training. Content and collaborator interactions are organized into a narrative structure of sequenceable stories rendered on axis-based graphical timelines, where artifacts, events, and collaborator states are indexed, linked, and tokenized. Behavioral signals extracted from the narrative context are used to (i) enrich prompt construction and retrieval-augmented generation, (ii) curate and contextualize training datasets, and (iii) propose context-aware AI agents and interventions. The storytelling interface aligns visual, temporal, and relational cues with machine-learning workflows to produce narratively grounded behavioral data for fine-tuning models and enabling context-sensitive information navigation.

sources.title: SYSTEMS AND METHODS FOR VISION-LANGUAGE MODELS OF AGENTIC OPERATIONS [US20260350361A1]
sources.abstract: Embodiments described herein provide a reinforcement learning (RL)-based framework to fine-tune VLMs for agent tasks such that the finetuned VLM may produce outputs that align with agent tasks (toward achieving success in the designated task) by optimizing the VLM's decision-making behavior within an environment. Specifically, the training framework may adopt offline RL techniques-filtered supervised fine-tuning (FSFT)—which selectively filters demonstration datasets using a learned value model. Unlike standard offline RL methods, the training framework uses FSFT to surpass its demonstrations while remaining identical to SFT when data quality is high. Additionally, FSFT enables seamless data collection for further improvement, making it a low-risk, high-reward alternative to SFT in VLM agent training

sources.title: SYSTEM AND METHOD FOR ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE BASED BEHAVIORAL FACIAL RECOGNITION [US20260351043A1]
sources.abstract: A system and method for integrating facial recognition with artificial intelligence (AI) behavioral analysis by analyzing facial images using micro-expressions, emotional markers and psychodynamic interpretations and generating an investigative dossier of behavioral facial recognition. Using a specially configured application-specific AI model and specific data architectures and data sets facial behavioral analysis is conducted that is capable of interpreting images (e.g., static images) of the human face and producing a detailed behavioral report by using micro-expressions, emotional markers and psychodynamic interpretations. Through the specially configured application-specific AI model a functional specialization process is deployed that combines supervised fine-tuning, instruction-based adaptation (i.e., instruction tuning) and integration of specialized domain knowledge wherein the AI model has a modular architecture comprised of multiple AI microservices that are specifically designed for the identification, classification and interpretation of behavioral facial traits.

sources.title: MODIFYING WELLBORE LOGS WITH POOR DATA QUALITY [US20260350275A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    A method for modifying well log data with poor quality includes receiving input data. The method also includes identifying low-quality intervals in the input data having a quality that is below a quality threshold. Identifying the low-quality intervals includes determining a borehole rugosity based upon a first subset of the input data. The method also includes fine-tuning a pre-trained model based upon the low-quality intervals to produce a fine-tuned model.

sources.title: MEMORY REDUCTION IN FINE-TUNING AND TRAINING OF MACHINE LEARNING MODELS [WO2026231229A1]
sources.abstract: Systems and techniques are described herein for deployment of machine learning networks. For example, a computing device can obtain a representation of similarities between embeddings of a plurality of embeddings and additional embeddings of the plurality of embeddings, wherein each embedding corresponds to a term associated with a vocabulary of a machine learning network; determine, based on a plurality of terms corresponding to a target sequence of tokens and a subset of terms, a reduced vocabulary of the machine learning network, wherein the subset of terms are determined based on similarities between an embedding of each token of the target sequence and each term; determine one or more logits based on a layer of the machine learning network and the reduced vocabulary of the machine learning network; and determine, based on the reduced vocabulary, a probability distribution representing probabilities of subsequent tokens from the target sequence of tokens.

sources.title: MULTIMODAL LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS FOR DRIVING [US20260350408A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    A pretrained multimodal language model is integrated with specific tools specializing in specific capabilities which the pretrained multimodal language model lacks. The pretrained multimodal language model is fine-tuned to operate with the specific tools based on fine-tuning training data generated with a large language model separate from the pretrained multimodal language model. The fine-tuned pretrained multimodal language model receives a multimodal input relating to the specific capabilities which the multimodal language model lacks. The fine-tuned pretrained multimodal language model operates with the specific tools to generate a final output based on the multimodal input received by the fine-tuned pretrained multimodal language model.

sources.title: QUANTUM-RESISTANT ATTESTED KEY AND MODEL LIFECYCLE MANAGEMENT SYSTEM [US20260352451A1]
sources.abstract: [0000]    A quantum-resistant system manages the key and model lifecycle of an artificial intelligence model within a trusted execution environment (TEE). A key management engine generates, seals, rotates, and revokes post-quantum keys bound to a hardware-rooted measurement. A secure model update module applies attested changes linking a prior state to a new state. A verifiable fine-tuning module binds, as a single signed unit, digests of training data, gradients, and resulting weights to the measurement. A tamper-evident provenance ledger records the operations and may anchor digests to a public blockchain. The system may mint a self-sovereign agent identity for consumption by a separate orchestration subsystem. Keys, updates, and evidence exist unencrypted only within the TEE and are tamper-evidently bound to the measurement, so an operator cannot alter or suppress them without invalidating the attestation.

sources.title: COMPUTER-IMPLEMENTED METHOD FOR ESTIMATING THE TRANSFERABILITY OF PRUNED NEURAL NETWORK MODELS, IN PARTICULAR PRUNED BACKBONES, FOR A DOWNSTREAM TASK [WO2026229904A1]
sources.organization: SISVEL TECH S R L, UNIV DEGLI STUDI DI TORINO, INST MINES TELECOM
sources.abstract: A computer-implemented method for estimating the transferability of pruned neural network models for a downstream task, the method comprising: - receiving a plurality of pre-trained neural network models, each model having been pruned to reduce complexity; - for each pruned model, extracting feature representations from a dataset associated with the downstream task using the pruned model as an encoder; - applying a clustering algorithm to the extracted feature representations to form clusters corresponding to target classes, wherein the clustering algorithm operates without utilizing labels from the downstream task; - calculating a transferability score for each pruned model based on the alignment of the formed clusters with the known target classes, the transferability score being indicative of the model's suitability for the downstream task; - ranking the pruned models based on their respective transferability scores; selecting a pruned model from the ranked models as a candidate for deployment or further fine-tuning on the downstream task based on its transferability score.

sources.title: DYNAMIC CONTROL SYSTEM FOR COORDINATING PRODUCTION OF STREPTOMYCES SECONDARY METABOLITES AND USE THEREOF [WO2026228792A1]
authors: INST OF MICROBIOLOGY OF THE CHINESE ACADEMY OF SCIENCES
sources.organization: UNIV EAST CHINA SCIENCE & TECH, INST OF MICROBIOLOGY OF THE CHINESE ACADEMY OF SCIENCES
sources.abstract: The present invention provides a dynamic control system for coordinating the production of Streptomyces secondary metabolites and a use thereof. First, a universal artificial promoter PQS (trigger) responsive to multiple Streptomyces quorum-sensing systems is designed. A stabilizer is then constructed on the basis of a bistable gene circuit to convert transient signal output into stable signal output, thereby successfully eliminating dependence on inducers. Finally, an orthogonal amplifier is developed on the basis of a rare extracytoplasmic function σ factor of Streptomyces, and a library of different promoter elements responsive to the amplifier and spanning an approximately 535-fold strength range from weak to strong is constructed. The amplifier is combined with a CRISPRi system to construct an inverter, thereby achieving gene expression repression with a strength range of approximately 200-fold. The combination of the amplifier, the promoter library, and the inverter is referred to as an effector, providing abundant elements for fine-tuning target gene expression. The combination of the trigger, the stabilizer, and the effector is referred to as a Streptomyces multiplexed artificial control system (SMARTS), enriching control tools for Streptomyces.

draft.summary: Research on supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is growing very fast. Code-computed counts of papers using the exact phrase went from 635 in 2024 to 2,013 in 2025, and the year-to-date count is still rising (1,628 to 4,482 against the same dates last year). Patent publications are also rising (61% year to date), and SFT appears as a standard stage in post-training recipes and in vertical applications (S3, S7, P1, P2, X3). Commercial evidence is thin and mostly indirect: Alibaba offers a fine-tuning platform (M1), and Innodata's data-services business positions around SFT demand (M2). Risk findings, and Risk challenges that downgrade several Science findings (C1-C8), show that the evidence on diversity loss, data selection and mechanisms is weaker than first stated. Catastrophic forgetting and possible displacement by RL, LoRA or prompting are unresolved (R1, R2, R6, R7). The main uncertainty is whether SFT stays a core, value-capturing step or becomes a commodity stage inside broader post-training pipelines. SFT is a technique, not a product, and none of the evidence shows revenue attributable to it.
draft.plain_summary: Supervised fine-tuning means teaching an existing AI model new skills or behaviours by showing it many worked examples. Research and patent filings on it are growing very fast and it is widely used, but there is little hard evidence yet on who earns money from it. The main thing that could stop it is that it can make models forget what they already knew, and newer training methods may replace it in some uses.

themes.name: SFT limitations: catastrophic forgetting and competing adaptation methods

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: Standard SFT is repeatedly reported to degrade prior capabilities, and many proposed fixes add complexity or leave a gap (R1, R6). Full SFT may forget more than LoRA or in-context learning in data-scarce settings (R7, low confidence). Evidence is mostly preprint abstracts, so near-term practice may change before the science settles.

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: RL forgets less but adapts more slowly and costs more engineering and compute (R2), so a hybrid or mixed on-policy approach is plausible. Many competing mitigation methods exist (S2), but Risk challenges say they target different problems and rest on self-reported preprints (C2). Which approach wins is unknown.

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: The cited evidence does not address 3-5 year outcomes. Forgetting also depends on pretraining history and learning-rate settings outside the fine-tuning dataset (R3), and safety fixes may need to be applied at base-model training (R5), so outcomes depend on base-model producers.

bull.label: forecast
bull.narrative: Practical mitigations such as mixing on-policy data or anchoring and regularisation methods mature and are reproduced. SFT becomes safe and cheap to apply without losing earlier capabilities (S2, R6).

base.label: forecast
base.narrative: SFT continues to be used alongside RL and parameter-efficient methods. Forgetting is managed with added pipeline complexity rather than eliminated, and the SFT-versus-RL trade-off stays open (R2, R6).

bear.label: forecast
bear.narrative: Forgetting and safety erosion prove hard to fix for third-party fine-tuners. RL, LoRA or prompting replace full SFT in many uses, and SFT-centred offerings lose relevance (R1, R5, R7).
